title: Dermatological Changes During Pregnancy, Labour and Puerperium
path: Dermatological Changes During Pregnancy, Labour and Puerperium

headings.title: Introduction to Dermatological Changes in Maternity
headings.content: Pregnancy induces profound systemic adaptations, with the integumentary system undergoing some of the most visible transformations. Nearly every woman experiences noticeable skin alterations during gestation, labour, and the puerperium. These changes stem from a complex interplay of hormonal surges, immunological shifts, and mechanical stretching. While many of these cutaneous variations are entirely benign and resolve spontaneously after delivery, others cause significant psychological distress or indicate underlying pathological states. Understanding the boundary between normal physiological shifts and specific dermatoses is vital for providing holistic maternal care in diverse clinical settings, including busy antenatal clinics across Nigeria.

headings.title: Physiological Hormonal Triggers and Skin Alterations
headings.content: The endocrine profile of a pregnant woman shifts dramatically, directly impacting cutaneous structures. Estrogen and progesterone levels rise progressively throughout gestation, stimulating melanocytes and altering vascular reactivity. Additionally, the placenta secretes high concentrations of **melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH)** and **adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)**. These elevated peptide hormones account for the generalized hyperpigmentation frequently observed in expectant mothers. Concurrently, increased levels of circulating corticosteroids contribute to altered connective tissue matrix production, predisposing the skin to structural changes like striae gravidarum.

headings.title: Common Physiological Pigmentation Changes
headings.content:
Hyperpigmentation affects up to ninety percent of pregnant individuals, appearing most prominently in areas naturally rich in melanin or exposed to friction. 

- **Linea nigra**: The linea alba darkens into a vertical pigmented streak running from the xiphisternum to the pubic symphysis, typically becoming noticeable around the second trimester.
- **Melasma**: Also known as the mask of pregnancy, this blotchy, symmetrical hyperpigmentation develops across the forehead, cheeks, and nose, exacerbated significantly by sunlight exposure.
- **Areolar darkening**: The nipples and surrounding areolae deepen in pigmentation, often developing secondary peripheral rings.

Reassurance regarding the gradual fading of these marks postpartum is a key nursing intervention.

headings.title: Vascular and Connective Tissue Manifestations
headings.content:
Expanded blood volume and high estrogen levels drive striking vascular phenomena throughout gestation. Small vessel proliferation and dilation lead to characteristic cutaneous signs:

| Feature | Clinical Appearance | Common Location | Course Postpartum |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Spider angiomas** | Tiny arterioles with radiating branching capillaries | Face, neck, upper chest | Usually resolves completely |
| **Palmar erythema** | Diffuse mottled redness on the palms | Thenar and hypothenar eminences | Fades rapidly after birth |
| **Striae gravidarum** | Atrophic pink, purple, or silvery linear scars | Abdomen, breasts, thighs | Permanent, though color fades |

Connective tissue changes occur as collagen fibers stretch and separate under mechanical and hormonal influence, creating permanent dermal stretch marks.

headings.title: Hair and Nail Modifications During Pregnancy
headings.content: Hair growth cycles shift noticeably during pregnancy due to hormonal influences that prolong the **anagen (growth)** phase. Consequently, fewer hairs enter the telogen (resting) phase, resulting in a thick, lustrous scalp mane. However, this protective mechanism reverses dramatically postpartum, leading to **telogen effluvium**—a sudden, alarming shedding of hair that peaks around two to four months after delivery. Nail plates may also display accelerated growth, increased brittleness, or longitudinal ridging, all of which are temporary and require no aggressive medical intervention.

headings.title: Specific Dermatoses of Pregnancy
headings.content:
Pruritic skin conditions unique to gestation can severely impact maternal well-being. 

- **Atopic eruption of pregnancy**: Includes eczema-like lesions starting early in gestation.
- **Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy (PEP)**: Characterized by intensely itchy urticarial papules and plaques within striae on the abdomen during the third trimester, sparing the umbilicus.
- **Pemphigoid gestationis**: A rare autoimmune blistering disorder presenting with severe periumbilical urticarial plaques that evolve into tense vesicles and bullae.
- **Intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy (ICP)**: Presents with generalized, intractable pruritus without a primary rash, typically worse on the palms and soles, carrying significant fetal risks.

headings.title: Skin Manifestations During Labour
headings.content: The intense physical exertion of labour triggers acute cutaneous responses. Diaphoresis becomes profuse due to hypermetabolism, muscular work, and autonomic nervous system activation. Flushing of the face and upper chest is common during the second stage secondary to Valsalva maneuvers and increased cardiac output. Furthermore, localized pressure from positioning during prolonged deliveries can cause transient erythema or edema over dependent body prominences. Nurses should monitor skin integrity during long labours, ensuring proper repositioning to prevent pressure injuries.

headings.title: Puerperal Skin Changes and Postpartum Recovery
headings.content: The immediate postpartum period initiates a rapid reversal of gestational endocrine changes. Diuresis occurs swiftly over the first week post-delivery, eliminating excess interstitial fluid and often resolving pregnancy-induced peripheral edema. Vascular lesions such as palmar erythema and spider angiomas regress as estrogen levels plummet. Hyperpigmented areas like the linea nigra and melasma fade slowly over subsequent months but may not disappear entirely. Surgical or laceration repair sites require careful assessment for signs of infection or hematoma formation as the perineum heals.

headings.title: Nursing Assessment and Patient Education
headings.content: Comprehensive nursing care encompasses systematic integumentary assessment across all stages of maternity. Nurses must inspect the skin during antenatal booking and follow-up visits, noting the distribution of rashes, evaluating pruritus severity, and differentiating harmless physiological variants from pathological dermatoses. Patient education should focus on reassuring mothers about expected changes, advising sun protection to minimize melasma darkening, and warning against harsh chemical skin-bleaching agents. Prompt identification of warning signs like severe nocturnal itching ensures timely referral and safeguarding of maternal-fetal health.
